etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English entere, enter, borrowed from Anglo-Norman entier, from Latin integrum, accusative of integer (“whole”), from Proto-Italic *əntagros (“untouched”). Doublet of entier and integer.

quote.citation: 1624, John Donne, “17. Meditation”, in Deuotions upon Emergent Occasions, and Seuerall Steps in My Sicknes: […], London:  […]  A[ugustine] M[atthews] for Thomas Iones, →OCLC, pages 415–416:
quote.text: No man is an Iland, intire of it ſelfe; euery man is a peece of the Continent, a part of the maine;  […]

definitions.definition: (botany) Having a smooth margin without any indentation.
(botany) Consisting of a single piece, as a corolla.
(complex analysis, of a complex function) Complex-differentiable on all of ℂ.

quote.citation: 2018, Markus Zusak, Bridge of Clay, page 423:
quote.text: On top of that, he was entire, which meant his bloodline could carry on.

quote.citation: c. 1596–1599 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Second Part of Henry the Fourth, […]”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene iv]:
quote.text: See now, whether pure fear and entire cowardice doth not make thee / wrong this virtuous gentlewoman to close with us.

quote.citation: 1702–1704, Edward [Hyde, 1st] Earl of Clarendon, “(please specify |book=I to XVI)”, in The History of the Rebellion and Civil Wars in England, Begun in the Year 1641. […], Oxford, Oxfordshire: Printed at the Theater, published 1707, →OCLC:
quote.text: No man had ever a heart more entire to the king.

quote.citation: 1595, Edmunde Spenser [i.e., Edmund Spenser], “[Amoretti.] Sonnet VI”, in Amoretti and Epithalamion. […], London:  […]  [Peter Short] for William Ponsonby, →OCLC:
quote.text: Depp is the wound, that dints the parts entire

definitions.definition: (now rare) The whole of something; the entirety.

quote.text: In the entire of the Poems we never hear of a merchant ship of the Greeks.

quote.citation: 1924, EM Forster, A Passage to India, Penguin, published 2005, page 19:
quote.text: ‘Then is the City Magistrate the entire of your family now?’

quote.citation: 2005, James Meek, The People's Act of Love, Canongate, published 2006, page 124:
quote.text: He asked why Hijaz was an entire. You know what an entire is, do you not, Anna? A stallion which has not been castrated.

definitions.definition: (philately) A complete envelope with stamps and all official markings: (prior to the use of envelopes) a page folded and posted.
Porter or stout as delivered from the brewery.
